findings.title: Core scope matches the slice plan entry precisely
findings.description: The "Included" list maps one-to-one to the plan's (109) text: padded 2D array replacing `list[NDArray[np.intp]]`, builder helper, rewrites of `CohesionForce`/`SeparationForce`/`AlignmentForce`/`MomentumForce`/`LeadershipForce`, the `BulkForce` protocol signature change, `tick.py` updates, and caller/test updates. Nothing from the plan is dropped; "Excluded" correctly defers the spatial query (105) and already-vectorized forces. Dependency directions are correct: it consumes `AgentState`, `BehavioralProfile`, `SpatialQuery.query_radius` (100/101/102) and the frontmatter `parent` correctly points at the slice-plan document.

findings.title: Breaking `BulkForce` change is not coordinated with slice 103, which is designed against the old signature
findings.description: This slice makes a breaking change to the `BulkForce.__call__` signature (`neighbor_lists: list[NDArray[np.intp]]` → `neighbors: NeighborData`). But the already-written 103 design (predator-prey, `not_started`) is built on the *old* signature: it states "No changes to tick()" and "Forces receive the same `(state, neighbor_lists, profiles, active_indices)` arguments," and its `FlightForce`/`PursuitForce` sketches index into `neighbor_lists`. The slice plan lists 103's only dependency as (101), not 109, and the `parent` field does not make 103 depend on 109. The 109 frontmatter lists `103-predator-prey-dynamics` under `interfaces`, showing awareness, but neither document records a sequencing rule or a plan to re-baseline 103's force sketches to `NeighborData`. If 103 lands before 109, its two new forces will be written against a signature 109 then breaks and must be reworked; if 109 lands first, 103 must be updated to consume `NeighborData`. The gap the requirement leaves unmet: the architecture "Clean boundaries — internal representation choices … are replaceable without affecting consumers" and the plan's expectation that "all existing implementations and callers update in the same slice" are both undermined by an undocumented, out-of-scope consumer (103) that will silently break. Add an explicit note that 103's forces must target the post-109 `NeighborData` signature, or that 109 must also update 103's design/sketch.

findings.title: World-server-side `BulkForce` implementors (308/314) are affected but only implicitly named
findings.description: The "Technical Decisions" note that non-neighbor forces (`WorldBoundsRepulsor`, `ConstantDrift`, `VelocityDrag`) "accept the new parameter but ignore it." `WorldBoundsRepulsor` (slice 314, complete, world-server initiative) and the `force_builder` registry (slice 308) are concrete, already-merged `BulkForce` consumers that must be signature-updated when this slice lands, yet they belong to a different initiative. The "Included" item "Update to all callers and tests that construct or consume `BulkForce`" and the plan's "all existing implementations and callers update in the same slice" do cover this, so it is not dropped scope — but the doc never names the world-server test files and the `force_builder`/`WorldBoundsRepulsor` call sites as in-scope. The requirement left unmet: the plan's "callers update in the same slice" cannot be verified complete without an explicit statement that the world-server-side force implementors and their tests are included (or explicitly deferred with a follow-up). Recommend one sentence naming `migratory_server/force_builder.py`, `WorldBoundsRepulsor`, and the server test suite as updated in this slice, to avoid the cross-initiative break being discovered during 109's run.

findings.title: Parent "Tick determinism" NFR is not restated or verified
findings.description: The slice rewrites the hot path and introduces new per-tick array allocation (`NeighborData`, padded arrays, masked gathers). The parent architecture lists **Tick determinism** as a first-class design goal ("Given the same state and inputs, a tick produces the same outputs"). This slice doc never mentions determinism — not in Value, Success Criteria, or the Verification Walkthrough. The behavioral-equivalence test compares old-vs-new on *one* shared input, and "full test suite passes" does not assert that repeated identical ticks produce bit-identical output. The specific target the gap leaves unmet: a regression guarantee that the vectorized path is deterministic across repeated ticks (no NaN-from-uninitialized-memory, no ordering sensitivity in the padded/masked reduction). Add a success criterion + a repeated-tick determinism assertion (identical initial state → `np.array_equal` across two runs) mirroring slice 100's `TestDeterminism`.

findings.title: `NeighborData.mask` is redundant with `indices`
findings.description: The doc defines `mask[i,j] = True iff j < counts[i]` *and* defines `indices[i, counts[i]:] = -1`, and states padding is "never dereferenced thanks to `mask`." The mask is a pure, deterministic function of `indices` (`indices != -1`) and of `counts`, so storing a third `(n_active, max_neighbors)` boolean array duplicates state that a later slice (105 batch query, GPU offload) could recompute. This is minor and the doc already prefers simplicity, but dropping `mask` and deriving it (or relying on `counts`/the `-1` sentinel) would reduce the memory footprint and the number of things that must stay in sync. Not blocking; flag for proportionality.

findings.title: "Constant Python overhead regardless of agent count" is a claim about the plan, not what the padded-array design guarantees at the target scale
findings.description: The Overview states "force computation cost … with constant Python overhead, regardless of agent count or clustering density." The doc's own "Padded Array vs. Sparse/COO" decision concedes that at 100K+ a CSR representation "may become necessary," and a padded `(n_active, max_neighbors)` gather scales total work with `n_active × max_neighbors`. So the *Python-overhead* is O(1), but total CPU cost is not constant in agent count; at the architecture's "tens of thousands" target, memory for the padded arrays (indices, mask, gathered positions/velocities per force) and per-force O(n·k) NumPy work can approach the 50ms budget. The slice's actual deliverable — the observed 100-agent overrun fix within the 50ms budget — is sound, but the headline "regardless of agent count or clustering density" overstates what this design guarantees. Recommend anchoring the acceptance criterion to the 50ms budget at the validated 100-agent default (which the doc does in the Value/Verification sections) and explicitly bounding the guarantee, rather than implying unbounded constant time. This is inherited from the plan's own wording, so it is a precision nit, not a scope-creep finding.

findings.title: Minor: verification command uses a non-path `--config` value
findings.description: Step 2 of the Verification Walkthrough runs `python -m migratory_server --config default`, whereas every other slice uses `--config config/default.yaml` (300, 301, 305, 313, 314). If `default` is not a resolvable path/alias in the server's config loader, the step will fail. Cosmetic, but it is the doc's primary runtime-verification step for the NFR claim; align it with the established `--config config/default.yaml` form.

findings.title: Self-exclusion and zero-neighbor handling preserve current force semantics
findings.description: Moving self-exclusion from per-force `neighbors[neighbors != agent_idx]` filters into `build_neighbor_data` is behavior-preserving: slice 101 established self-inclusion as the `BruteForceQuery` default that every force filters, so centralizing the filter does not change which neighbors any force sees. The zero-neighbor case (`counts[i]==0`, full-`False` row → zero force) matches the documented per-force `if len(neighbors)==0: continue` guards, and `np.maximum(counts[:,None],1)` prevents division by zero in the cohesion/alignment masked means. `MomentumForce` is correctly treated as neighbor-independent. This keeps the slice's "behavioral equivalence" claim credible and is explicitly covered by success criteria.
